name: South Gate City Council
minutes_text:
CITY OF SOUTH GATE
  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MINUTES
  TUESDAY, MARCH 10, 2026
CALL TO ORDER  Joshua Barron, Mayor called a Regular City Council Meeting to order at
  6:52 p.m.

INVOCATION  Tina De La Rosa, Acting Director of Parks & Recreation
PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk

ROLL CALL  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk

PRESENT  Mayor Joshua Barron, Vice Mayor Al Rios, Council Member Maria del
  Pilar Avalos; and City Treasurer Jose De La Paz, City Manager Rob
  Houston, City Attorney Raúl F. Salinas

ABSENT/EXCUSED  Council Member Gil Hurtado and Council Member Maria Davila

PRESENTATION

1
BUDGET ADMIN  The City Council approved items A, B, & C by motion of Vice Mayor
  Rios and seconded by Mayor Barron:

  a. Received the Fiscal Year 2025-26 Mid-Year Budget Report and
  Adjustments;

  b. Approved the Fiscal Year 2025-26 Mid-Year Adjustments; and

  c. Adopted Resolution No. 2026-07-CC entitled A Resolution of the City
  of South Gate approving Fiscal Year 2025-26 Mid-Year Budget
  Amendments and Adjustments.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes (voted no on items B and C);
  Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor Barron, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  excused; Council Member Davila, excused.
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

PUBLIC HEARINGS

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING  Following the conclusion of the Public Hearing, the City Council:

  a. Adopted Resolution No. 2026-08-CC entitled A Resolution of the City
  Council of the City of South Gate, approving Substantial Amendment
  No. 2 to the Fiscal Year 2023-2024 Annual Action Plan; Substantial
  Amendment No. 2 to the Fiscal Year 2024-2025 Annual Action Plan;
  and Substantial Amendment No. 1 to Fiscal Year 2025-2026 Annual
  Action Plan Reprogramming Community Development Block Grant
  (CDBG);

  b. Authorized the City Manager or the Community Development
  Director to initiate appropriate action necessary to implement projects
  and programs as noted in the FY 2025-2026 Annual Action Plan; and

  c. Reallocated $749,254 in Community Development Block Grant
  (CDBG) funds and $340,000 in HOME Investment Partnerships
  Program (HOME) funds from current activity allocations to the
  proposed budget amendments within each respective fund.

  Gabriel Perez, Director of Community Development, explained that this
  item concerns the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds,
  which are federal HUD funds allocated to the City annually. The City has
  discretion in programming these funds, and the City Council has
  previously reviewed the Annual Action Plan for this year’s allocation.
  Today’s item is a proposed substantial amendment needed to begin
  expending the funds. Mr. Perez noted that Ana Marie LeNoue, the City’s
  contracted program consultant, will present the details.

  Ana Marie LeNoue, President of Advanced Avant-Garde Corporation,
  delivered the presentation.

  Mr. Perez reported that the City is considering reallocating a portion of its
  CDBG funds for a demolition project involving the Housing Authority
  properties at 9001 and 9019 Long Beach Boulevard. The intent is to
  prepare the site for future sales and the development of fourteen affordable
  town homes by Habitat for Humanity. The project is currently undergoing
  environmental review and will be presented to the Planning Commission
  and City Council at a later date.

  Mayor Barron asked if anyone in the audience wished to speak on this
  item.

  Robyn Logan of Hunt Avenue inquired about the potential value of a
  townhome and its implications for property tax revenue for the city.

  Page 2 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  Edgar Pelayo of Mallison Avenue asked for clarification on the rationale
  for reallocating funds to other projects and whether the same process is
  used during initial allocations. He stated that involving commissions and
  residents in these decisions would enhance transparency, accountability,
  and community trust by ensuring that information is clearly
  communicated.

  Jimmy Ozaeta, South Gate resident, provided a detailed report at the most
  recent City Council meeting. He noted that significant advocacy efforts
  have sought to reallocate approximately one million dollars from this
  funding to support Parks and Recreation programs. He also expressed
  concern that portions of the funding were reallocated due to ongoing
  timeliness issues. Mr. Ozaeta recommended reassessing the factors
  contributing to these delays and suggested directing the funds toward
  street and sidewalk improvements.

EMAILS  Mario Dominguez expressed concern that the $1.1 million and CDBG
  funds allocated in March 2025 for Parks and Recreation projects were not
  advanced prior to the former director’s retirement. He criticized city
  leadership and staff for what he considers inadequate oversight and
  accountability in ensuring the timely completion of projects intended to
  benefit residents.

  Having no one else come forward, Mayor Barron closed the audience
  portion.

  Councilwoman Avalos asked if the City of South Gate is currently in a
  workout plan with HUD.

  Ms. LeNoue replied in the affirmative.

  Councilwoman Avalos asked if the city has $2.2 million right now.

  Ms. LeNoue replied in the affirmative.

  Councilwoman Avalos stated that the CAC reviewed and allocated the
  funding. She recalled making the motion to allocate $50,000 to support
  small businesses when the item previously came before the Council. She
  noted that these funds appear to have been redirected despite small
  businesses continuing to face financial challenges due to recent ICE raids
  and current economic conditions. She requested that the funds remain
  allocated as originally approved and that the program be initiated.

  She also referenced the commercial façade program, noting that many
  businesses are interested in making improvements, but the city has

  Page 3 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  indicated these projects are not currently feasible. She requested that
  $200,000 remain allocated to the commercial façade program.

  She acknowledged that both the city’s sidewalks and roadways are in poor
  condition.

  Vice Mayor Rios noted that these are HUD funds used for various projects
  and asked whether the CAC had approved the recommendation.

  Ms. LeNoue stated that the new recommendations were presented to the
  CAC for feedback, and the committee accepted the presentation without
  offering any changes.

  Vice Mayor Rios requested clarification on the total funding required for
  the housing project.

  Mr. Perez stated that Habitat will request approximately $1.6 million in
  HOME funds from the City, with additional support anticipated through
  PHA funding. The estimated construction cost for the project is $11.8
  million. Habitat has submitted its application, which will undergo review
  by the Planning Commission. The City Council will subsequently review
  the tentative tract map for the townhomes.

  Councilwoman Avalos inquired whether the city owns the property and
  whether it intends to provide funding to the developer for the project’s
  construction.

  Mr. Perez noted that while the City can provide HOME funds, any
  allocation would require future City Council approval.

  Vice Mayor Rios inquired about who will manage the housing project
  upon its completion and whether Habitat will assume responsibility. He
  also expressed interest in giving South Gate residents priority.

  Mr. Perez noted that limiting eligibility to South Gate residents presents
  certain challenges.

  Ms. LeNoue asked whether the question referred to which households may
  apply for the housing program. Eligibility is based on household income
  and is open to low-and-moderate income households, not limited to South
  Gate residents.

  Mayor Barron concurred with Councilwoman Avalos that addressing small
  business needs should remain a priority. He expressed concern regarding
  the façade improvement program, noting that property owners are the
  primary beneficiaries of such enhancements.

  Page 4 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  Ms. LeNoue stated that while a tenant may request the funds, the property
  owner must authorize the improvements and provide access to the
  property.

  Mayor Barron noted that the city’s most significant success was the gift
  card program, which provided meaningful benefits to both local
  businesses and residents.

  Ms. LeNoue stated that HUD does not allow the use of gift cards for
  program purposes.

  Ms. LeNoue provided information regarding the small business assistance
  program. A business may qualify if it is located within a low-income
  census tract, which includes most of the city. Eligible uses of the funds
  include job creation or qualifying capital purchases. The City would need
  to determine the grant amount, and recipients would be required to provide
  documentation verifying that the funds were used for eligible expenses.
  This program could be implemented as described.

  Mayor Barron clarified that the funding could not be used to help
  businesses cover their operating expenses.

  Ms. LeNoue stated that if the business needed to purchase a refrigerator,
  the expense would qualify as capital purchase.

  Councilwoman Avalos asked whether those funds could be used to cover
  an employee’s salary.

  Ms. LeNoue confirmed that funding may be approved if the business can
  demonstrate a loss of revenue and show that the funds will be used to
  cover the employee’s salary. She noted that employment-based funding
  requires the employee to meet low-to-moderate income household criteria,
  which obligates the employer to collect extensive personal information.
  Based on her experience with similar programs, many employees are
  reluctant to provide the required documentation.

  Rob Houston, City Manager, explained that staff reviewed the proposed
  $50,000 small business program and identified several significant
  limitations. The previous gift card initiative was funded through ARPA,
  which allowed much greater flexibility, whereas CDBG funds are highly
  restricted.

  He noted that administering such a program would require dedicated staff
  to verify eligibility, track distributions, and review required financial
  documentation. The estimated administrative cost alone would be
  approximately $20,000, leaving only $30,000 for direct assistance.
  Page 5 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  Mr. Houston added that determining which businesses qualify—and how
  to fairly allocate limited funds—would be challenging. For example,
  providing $1,000 per business would help only about 30 businesses,
  leaving many without support. Additionally, participation would require
  businesses to submit detailed financial records, such as tax information,
  which some may be unwilling to provide.

  Mayor Barron noted several of the revitalization grants and acknowledged
  that they are intended for substantial home improvement projects that
  enhance property value.

  He asked how the property could be demolished without delays and how
  to move the project forward.

  He noted that a resident raised a valid point about ensuring our quotes are
  obtained as accurately and efficiently as possible, given how quickly
  prices can change.

  Mr. Houston explained that Parks and Recreation staff identify projects
  and make every effort to advance them to the bidding stage. However,
  ongoing budget cuts and citywide hiring freeze have made it difficult to
  sustain project work, as vacant positions cannot be filled without
  additional revenue. As a result, these projects are being forwarded to
  Public Works Engineering, which has also experienced reductions in staff.
  Consequently, many city projects are expected to progress more slowly.

  Mr. Houston noted that the commercial rehabilitation program has been
  somewhat disappointing. Initially, the city intended to develop a strong
  plan to support businesses in improving their façades. Unlike previous
  approaches, where a single business could receive up to $100,000, the
  current proposal distributes funds along sections of Tweedy Boulevard,
  offering a maximum of $7,000–$10,000 per business with a required 50
  percent match to ensure landlord participation. The project is currently on
  hold due to budget reductions and the loss of two code enforcement
  officers.

  Mayor Barron acknowledged the established process the City follows with
  its commissions. While commissioners provide recommendations on the
  use of funds, final decisions rest with the Council, which must deliberate
  and act in the best interest of the community. He emphasized the
  importance of communication and commended staff for their thorough
  presentation to the CAC. He also thanked staff for reporting that the CAC
  had no concerns, noting that the required 30-day review period has been
  concluded and the Council is now prepared to make its decision.

  Page 6 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  Councilwoman Avalos moved to approve the item with the following
  amendments: allocate $100,000 to small businesses, $100,000 to the
  commercial façade program, $800,000 to city streets, and distribute the
  remaining funds as designated by staff.

  Mr. Houston asked whether the Council has identified any items they no
  longer wish to fund.

  Ms. LeNoue stated staff will need to pull funds from the current activity
  allocation line because the proposed changes totaled less than $800,000.

  Arturo Cervantes, Director of Public Works, noted that he welcomes
  additional funding for the city’s roadway projects. He explained that the
  recently received $750,000 must be spent within the next two to three
  months, and the department is working quickly to allocate those funds.
  However, adding another $800,000 at this time would not ensure the city’s
  ability to use the money effectively. Public Works is currently limited in
  staffing and resources, and additional street projects require engineering
  work before they can proceed. Mr. Cervantes stated he cannot commit to
  spending the additional $800,000 by the May deadline. The department is
  able to utilize the current $750,000 only because it is being applied to an
  existing street project already underway. He is uncertain how the
  department could responsibly spend the extra $800,000 within the required
  timeframe.

  Councilwoman Avalos asked whether any additional streets have been
  identified for restricting.

  Mr. Cervantes noted that while many city streets require investment, the
  improvement process involves several steps: identifying priority streets,
  hiring a consultant for design, soliciting bids, and ultimately completing
  construction.

  Councilwoman Avalos noted that one of the streets she had in mind runs
  parallel to Firestone, specifically Truba Avenue, which contains a small
  section of recently smoothed pavement.

  Mr. Cervantes noted that Truba presents a unique challenge. Designing the
  project to meet ADA requirements will take the city approximately six
  months. He added that the Frontage Road project required nearly a year to
  complete the full process and construction.

  Mr. Houston explained that there are essentially two timelines. The city
  has an immediate need this year to prepare projects for implementation,
  while the annual allocation process determines priorities for future
  funding. If a majority of the Council wishes to shift next year’s funding

  Page 7 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  emphasis, for example, placing greater priority on roadway improvements
  rather than specific project staff can adjust accordingly and bring revised
  recommendations to the CAC for the next funding cycle. He noted that
  this may involve re-evaluating or deferring some planned projects.
  However, he also emphasized that there are practical limits to how quickly
  the city can pivot, as outlined by the Public Works Director.

  Mayor Barron requested clarification, noting that the Truba project is
  already listed as a street identified for needed improvements.

  Mr. Cervantes responded that it is not. He explained that the city uses a
  pavement management system to prioritize street repairs over a five-year
  period. In the area referenced by the Councilwoman, all prioritized streets
  have already been addressed. Truba Avenue was not identified as a
  priority, and several other streets citywide rank higher for future
  investment. If additional funding were available, he would recommend
  allocating it to those higher-priority locations. Truba is not included in the
  near-term Capital Improvement Program. However, if the Council wishes
  to elevate it as a policy priority, the department would be prepared to
  proceed accordingly.

  Mayor Barron requested that the Council receive, at a future date, an
  explanation of the criteria used to determine street-prioritization decisions.

  Mr. Cervantes responded in the affirmative.

  The Councilwoman inquired about which other streets are eligible and
  ready for funding.

  Mr. Cervantes noted that the department has no additional street projects
  ready for implementation within the next three months. He added that the
  City’s Pavement Management System identifies more than $80 million in
  needed funding to address street repairs citywide.

  Mayor Barron asked whether it would be possible to schedule an off-site
  meeting for the Councilwoman to meet with the Public Works
  Department, review their processes, assess the streets included in the
  program, and receive a related presentation.

  Mr. Cervantes responded in the affirmative.

  Mayor Barron stated that all council should also receive the report.

  Councilwoman Avalos requested clarification regarding the $513,000
  allocation in the current fiscal year’s budget.

  Page 8 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  Ms. LeNoue stated that the amount presented totaled $758,990.

  Councilwoman Avalos asked when the funds must be spent.

  Ms. LeNoue responded within three months. The city is working to fully
  utilize the available funding in coordination with Public Works. The
  project is already underway, and the funding allocation is being increased
  from $513,000 to $758,000.

  Councilwoman Avalos asked whether the funds could be directed toward
  areas lacking sidewalks, in addition to the previously identified funding.

  Mr. Cervantes explained that the city faces more than twenty million
  dollars in needed sidewalk repairs. He noted that the process is lengthy, as
  Public Works must procure a designer, identify and survey the affected
  locations, develop the project plans, and issue the work for bid.

  Mr. Houston asked whether any of the proposed projects are unacceptable
  and should not be funded. If all projects are recommended, no additional
  funds would be available for reallocation. However, if some projects are
  deemed unsuitable, staff can evaluate how much funding could be
  redirected and whether it can be programmed elsewhere. He added that
  staff cannot meet the May deadline for sidewalk and street projects this
  year, but there will be significantly more opportunity to address these
  needs in next year’s allocation.

  Mr. Cervantes confirmed this.

  Mayor Barron noted that Councilwoman Avalos has requested the
  reallocation of one million dollars and asked Councilwoman Avalos to
  identify where those funds could be drawn from.

  Councilwoman Avalos responded that the funds would come from the 2.2
  million.

  Vice Mayor Rios noted that since the city is unable to complete the
  sidewalk project, the remaining $400,000 allocations could potentially be
  used elsewhere. He emphasized that Truba is an important street, serving
  as a main thoroughfare, and pointed out that the surrounding streets on the
  west side have already been improved.

  Mr. Houston suggested revisiting the street improvement topic in the
  future, possibly with a presentation explaining the process for assessing
  road conditions and prioritizing repairs across different neighborhoods.
  However, these discussions cannot be included in this year’s CDBG
  funding due to time constraints. Staff are seeking direction soon, as

  Page 9 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  projects recommended for completion by May must remain feasible within
  the current timeline.

  Vice Mayor Rios inquired whether it would be feasible to complete the
  other two projects referenced for the $100,000 by May.

  Mr. Houston noted that while a small business program is possible,
  determining eligibility, restrictions, and administrative costs is complex.
  With limited staff and ongoing budget cuts and labor changes, he doubts
  the team can take on a new project or complete it by May.

  Councilwoman Avalos acknowledged that more time would have been
  helpful, but since allocations from July last year were not addressed, she
  proposes allocating $150,000 to small business and reducing the
  neighborhood revitalization grant program to $75,000.

  Vice Mayor Rios asked Ms. LeNoue whether that solution would be
  acceptable.

  Ms. LeNoue confirmed it is possible, but the requested funds for the
  neighborhood revitalization grant program are needed to process current
  applications. Transferring $75,000 would likely lead to cuts.

  Councilwoman Avalos announced a $75,000 addition to the neighborhood
  revitalization grant program.

  Ms. LeNoue asked from which project.

  Councilwoman Avalos commented from the demolition and clearance
  process.

  Ms. LeNoue asked if the plan was to cancel the demolition and clearance
  project.

  Councilwoman Avalos responded in the affirmative.

  Ms. LeNoue said the request is to transfer funds from demolition and
  clearance, adding $75,000 to the neighborhood revitalization grant and
  $150,000 to small business.

  Councilwoman Avalos responded in the affirmative.

  Vice Mayor Rios asked, "What does that look like?"

  Mr. Houston explained that moving forward with the Long Beach
  townhomes relies on obtaining the full $225,000 to remove the current

  Page 10 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  building; otherwise, it will remain due to a lack of alternative funding
  sources. He expressed doubts about quickly establishing a business
  program, administering it, collecting and reviewing financial data, and
  allocating grants within three months before funds expire.

  Luis Frausto, Director of Administrative Services, said building 14
  properties will boost the city's property tax revenue. Though benefits won't
  appear immediately, planning ahead is key. The new properties, each
  worth at least $500,000, will strengthen the city's tax base.

  Councilwoman Avalos asked Ms. LeNoue if one employee is sufficient to
  run the small business program, and what the associated cost would be.

  Ms. LeNoue explained that her team manages small business programs for
  cities. They must develop guidelines, obtain council approval, which may
  take one to two months, and then implement the program. Key decisions
  include determining the funding amount for each business and establishing
  selection criteria.

  She has held discussions with the HUD representative, which have been
  beneficial for both the director and Ms. Averell, the Housing Manager.
  Additionally, the HUD representative is communicating on behalf of the
  city to the HUD Director, who is taking directives from the federation.
  Cities that have not spent all their allocated funds face significant
  challenges for various reasons. Until now, she had never encountered the
  possibility of losing future funding.

  Vice Mayor Rios acknowledged the value of the discussion and expressed
  appreciation for Councilwoman Avalos’ input and efforts to effect change.
  He noted that the matter concerns compliance and timeliness, and
  subsequently moved to adopt recommendation actions A, B, and C. Mayor
  Barron seconded the motion.

  Councilwoman Avalos inquired with Mr. Cervantes whether a demolition
  design plan is required.

  Mr. Cervantes said it often depends on the location, but in many instances,
  demolition does occur.

  Councilwoman Avalos inquired whether a design plan had been prepared
  for the demolition of the property.

  Mr. Cervantes does not have familiarity with the project. Could you please
  clarify what is being demolished?

  Ms. LeNoue states of an existing structure and then removing the soil.

  Page 11 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT’D  Mr. Cervantes inquired about the structure.

  Ms. LeNoue suggested that the Director of Community Development
  might be able to provide an explanation.

  Mr. Perez mentioned that the building has a base of approximately 200
  square feet.

  Mr. Cervantes explained that the process begins by hiring a consultant to
  create a demolition package, which is necessary for bidding. He noted that
  this documentation takes time and that three months is a short period in
  the public sector.

  Councilwoman Avalos said the project cannot proceed.

  Mr. Houston indicated that every effort will be made to ensure the
  project's progress. He noted that there is as much likelihood of completing
  this project as those other programs which have yet to begin and will
  require further review. He also observed that this demolition has already
  undergone some level of review and procedural evaluation.

  Mr. Perez noted that Ms. Averell has reviewed the matter and a draft RFP
  is ready. He recommends proceeding, as we have ongoing obligations to
  secure and clean these properties. If we cannot sell or repurpose the
  property, expenses will continue.

  ROLL CALL: Councilwoman Avalos, no; Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor
  Barron, yes; Council Member Hurtado, absent; Council Member Davila,
  absent.

3
PROPERTY USE
ADMIN/PERMITS  Following the conclusion of the Public Hearing, the City Council
  approved items A, B, & C by motion of Vice Mayor Rios and seconded by
  Mayor Barron:

  ROLL CALL: Councilwoman Avalos, yes; Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor
  Barron, yes; Council Member Hurtado, absent; Council Member Davila,
  absent.

  a. A finding that in accordance with CEQA, this project qualifies for a
  categorical exemption under CEQA Guidelines Section 15303 (Class
  3), “New Construction or Conversion of Small Structures,” and is
  thereby exempt from CEQA in that the subject property will continue
  to be used as a parking lot for a new drive-through restaurant;

  Page 12 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

3
PROPERTY USE
ADMIN/PERMITS CONT’D
  b. Resolution No. 2026-09-CC entitled A Resolution of the City Council
  of the City of South Gate, State of California, approving General Plan
  Amendment No. 25-01 for a property at 8915 Vossler Avenue; and

  c. Introduced Ordinance No. 2026-01-CC entitled An Ordinance of the
  City Council of the City of South Gate, State of California, approving
  Zone Change No. 25-01 for a property at 8915 Vossler Avenue.

  Gabriel Perez, Director of Community Development, stated that John
  Signo, Planning Manager, will be giving the presentation.

  John Signo, Planning Manager, gave the presentation.

  Mr. Houston noted that David Ghermezian, the property owner and
  developer, is available for questions and would also like to make a brief
  statement.

  Mayor Barron asked if anyone on the public would like to speak on this
  item and if any emails were received. Seeing no one coming up and not
  receiving any emails, Mayor Barron closed the audience portion.

  Mayor Barron asked Mr. Ghermezian to step up to the podium.

  Mr. Ghermezian has owned this property for approximately seven years.
  Throughout this period, the site has consistently operated as a restaurant,
  with the parking lot serving its patrons. The use of the property remains
  unchanged—the parking lot continues to support the development facing
  Firestone. Considerable thought has gone into designing the site.

  Councilwoman Avalos thanked Mr. Ghermezian and asked how soon
  construction would begin if approved, noting the property has been vacant
  for seven years.

  Mr. Ghermezian shared that previous city staff’s lack of understanding
  about the project, and the overlay zone caused him to lose tenants.
  However, the new staff have been supportive and provided helpful
  information. He is currently negotiating with tenants and hopes council
  will see a project within 12 months.

  Jose De La Paz, City Treasurer, raised a concern about the planning
  commission’s condition requiring 8915 Vossler to be attached to the
  restaurant parcel, preventing separate sale. This restriction suggests the lot
  can't operate independently under the new zoning and may indicate that
  the zoning change is tailored for the drive-thru project rather than city
  policy, as it removes a residential transition buffer for a single parcel.
  Page 13 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

3
PROPERTY USE
ADMIN/PERMITS CONT’D  He is concerned that the proposal resembles spot zoning and questions
  why rezoning is necessary if the parking lot remains unchanged.

  Vice Mayor Rios expressed his appreciation to Mr. Ghermezian for
  attending the meeting. He stated that the purpose of the zoning change
  appears to be facilitating the acquisition of a tenant but sought clarification
  regarding the rationale behind the implementation of a CEQA guideline.

  Vice Mayor Rios noted limited parking behind the building and inquired
  about the total spaces planned for the project.

  Mr. Ghermezian responded: 11 spaces in the rear lot.

  Mr. Houston explained that the back parking lot has served the business
  for years but is zoned residential under corridor zoning. The Vice Mayor
  questioned this designation, and Mr. Perez or Mr. Signo can clarify the
  zoning details. The corridor zone is meant to complement both
  commercial and residential areas; if combined with a commercial
  business, it may be eligible for rezoning pending council approval. Mr.
  Perez can provide further information on this matter.

  Mr. Perez stated Mr. Signo may speak on this.

  Mr. Signo supports the City Manager's view. The property has served as a
  parking lot for decades, but it was zoned residential, which is not
  appropriate. With a new project underway, the general plan amendment
  and zone change will correct this. Linking the parking lot to restaurant
  properties ensures that if ownership changes, the restaurant retains its
  parking spaces. This protects the parking area for future use.

  Mayor Barron believes only two corridors have that zoning: Tweedy and
  Firestone.

  Mr. De La Paz asked if the city is spot zoning?

  Mr. Signo does not consider this to be spot zoning, as the adjacent
  properties along Firestone are UN zoned commercials.

  Vice Mayor Rios indicated that no adverse effects are anticipated.

  Mr. Signo stated that CEQA includes a list of categorical exemptions
  available to the City. If a project qualifies under one of these exemptions,
  the City may rely on it to exempt the project from CEQA requirements.

  Vice Mayor Rios asked whether the project would block Firestone, noting
  that it is a thoroughfare.

  Page 14 of 26
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF MARCH 10, 2026

3
